Prices are pushing between $10-18/sqft in a city pushing a 200,000 population. Many neighboring small towns(within 15 miles are looking at between $3-8/sqft, which is still fairly expensive. Is this common? Will counties/townships even rezone agricultural land to commercial? Rural/agricultural land in this area is selling for $5,000-10,000 an acre on average. Even if I had to pay up to $25,000/acre, I feel like I'd be getting a hell of deal compared to the $360,000 for 4 acres, that's offered for sale in the empty industrial park, in one of the small neighboring towns.

Obviously anyone want their business next to a busy highway, but I don't NEED that. A large rural, and a massive suburban population exists, and almost any paved back road or highway is heavily traveled and have good traffic counts.

As a land owner(80acre+), would you be willing to sell 4 acres @ $25,000/acre(150% over largest market value)? If your county has its zoning regulations and maps online then you should me able to figure out whether your business would be allowed. Subdividing a property is a hassle, so that's going to be an extra obstacle while trying to convince some farmer to sell a portion of his land. There are websites that list land for sale, so if you can find something adequate that's already listed, I'd think that would be way easier to convince somebody to sell who isn't already looking to sell.
Leasing is possible but buying is often more hassle than its worth.

private real estate sales (unlisted in zillow, not For Sale signs, etc) are easy, way better than public sales, and have nearly the same success rate.

you can easily find affordable land most anywhere not urban. and owners of 'unused' property are generally flexible.

farm land though is not cheap or generally for sale. farms are active businesses who are investing in land. you want unused or dilapidated land for the best price, but you can make any kind of offer on any kind of property.

also, think about barter, and a small biz that is highly portable (like offices/factories that can be trailered).

zoning prohibitions are real, but not too hard to navigate or bend if you are not going to be disruptive and do a little homework.

A five minute conversation with a real estate company would tell you more than you need. Try to find one that deals with farms, farmland, or acreages in the area. They'll tell you about the zoning restrictions, give you an idea about the cost of getting electricity and gas to the site. And tell you many things you didn't even think of.
